paragraphs: Robert Baden-Powell (1857–1941) was the founder of the Boy Scouts. His experimental camp on Brownsea Island in 1907 and the publication of Scouting for Boys in 1908 laid the foundations of a worldwide youth movement. In 1920, at the first World Scout Jamboree, he was acclaimed Chief Scout of the World.

Before Scouting became his life’s work, Baden-Powell spent more than three decades in the British Army. Commissioned into the 13th Hussars in 1876, he served in India and Africa, took part in the Ashanti and Matabele campaigns, and became a national figure through the defence of Mafeking in 1899–1900. He later served as Inspector-General of Cavalry and rose to lieutenant-general. A highly decorated officer, he was appointed Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath and of the Royal Victorian Order. He retired from the army in 1910 to devote himself to Scouting; further honours followed, including a peerage in 1929 and the Order of Merit in 1937.

His ideas grew through practical experience and exchange with other pioneers. The American scout Frederick Russell Burnham helped shape his understanding of tracking and self-reliance in southern Africa. Ernest Thompson Seton, whom he met in 1906, brought the Woodcraft Indians and The Birch-Bark Roll into that conversation. Seton’s nature study and campcraft became an important influence on Scouting for Boys. Daniel Carter Beard’s Sons of Daniel Boone formed another strand of the American outdoor movement; Beard and Seton later helped build the Boy Scouts of America.

Baden-Powell’s books trace the passage from military reconnaissance to education through adventure. Aids to Scouting was written for soldiers; Scouting for Boys carried observation, resourcefulness, patrol work and service into a programme for young people. His campaign narratives show the officer and field observer whose experience preceded the Scout movement.

Born in Boston in 1823, Francis Parkman studied at Harvard and began planning a history of the struggle for North America. His writing brought together journeys through the country and the study of its documentary record, following the contest between France and England across the continent.

In 1846 he travelled from St. Louis into the Great Plains with his cousin Quincy Adams Shaw. Emigrant wagons, buffalo hunts, Fort Laramie and weeks among the Oglala supplied the material for his first book. The narrative appeared in the Knickerbocker Magazine before its publication as The California and Oregon Trail in 1849.

Parkman later became known for The Conspiracy of Pontiac and the series France and England in North America. The Discovery of the Great West, published in 1869 as the third part of that history, follows French exploration into the continental interior and La Salle’s journeys toward the Mississippi. Together, these books approach North America through the experiences of travellers and the ambitions of competing powers.
